name: Invoice Capture and Coding
title: Invoice Capture and Coding
answer: Invoice capture and coding covers the intake of supplier invoices from paper, PDF, email and electronic formats, the extraction of header and line item data, and the assignment of general ledger accounts, cost centres, tax codes and project or department dimensions. It also includes matching invoices to purchase orders and goods receipts, flagging duplicates and routing exceptions for review. In receivables, the same capture logic can be applied to customer remittances and billing documents, but the core use is in accounts payable.

crumbs.name: Knowledge Based Professions and their Future

sections.body: Invoice capture and coding covers the intake of supplier invoices from paper, PDF, email and electronic formats, the extraction of header and line item data, and the assignment of general ledger accounts, cost centres, tax codes and project or department dimensions. It also includes matching invoices to purchase orders and goods receipts, flagging duplicates and routing exceptions for review. In receivables, the same capture logic can be applied to customer remittances and billing documents, but the core use is in accounts payable.
sections.heading: Scope

sections.body: The work runs on document processing pipelines that combine optical character recognition, document classification and field extraction models with validation rules and an interface to the organisation's enterprise resource planning system. Invoices are typically ingested through email inboxes, supplier portals or scanning endpoints, then normalised into a structured record before coding. Many deployments use cloud-based accounts payable automation platforms, while some retain on-premise OCR for sensitive or high-volume environments.
sections.heading: What it runs on

sections.body: Extraction models identify supplier name, invoice number, date, amounts, tax and line item details, often with a confidence score for each field. Coding suggestions are generated from historical posting patterns, supplier master data and chart of accounts rules, and low-confidence or non-standard items are sent to a human reviewer. Purchase order matching compares extracted lines against open purchase orders and receipts, and the system learns from corrections that reviewers make over time.
sections.heading: How the work is done

sections.body: Invoice data is subject to financial controls, tax record keeping and data protection rules, so capture systems must keep an audit trail from original document to posted entry. Access to coding and approval workflows is usually separated by role to preserve segregation of duties, and duplicate or anomalous invoices are blocked for review. Retention of source documents and extracted data must follow the organisation's own compliance obligations, and model decisions should be explainable enough for internal audit and external review.
sections.heading: Rights, risk and provenance

sections.body: The direction is toward touchless processing, where a higher share of invoices is captured, coded and approved without manual intervention. E-invoicing mandates and supplier networks are pushing more structured data into the pipeline, reducing reliance on OCR. Generative models are beginning to draft coding explanations and handle unstructured supplier queries, while agentic workflows may eventually coordinate approval, payment and cash forecasting from a single captured invoice.
